text.tspan: entry point: parses the command, wires the parts together, starts the threads

text.font-family: Virgil, Segoe UI Emoji, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: This is the front door. When you type `nettap <something>`, the click library routes it to one function in this file. Some commands start a long-
running process: `watch` (one daemon on the host that captures many containers), `sidecar` (captures one container from inside that container's
network) and `sidecars` (a manager that starts and repairs sidecars for you). The others are quick one-shots: `attach` / `detach` only write a request
into the database for the running `watch` daemon to pick up, and `status` / `analyze` / `report` / `enrich` read the database, print, and exit. cli.py
does little work itself - it builds the pieces from the other modules, starts the background threads, and makes sure every tcpdump is stopped cleanly
OUT: running threads and tcpdump processes, rows in SQLite, printed text or an HTML file
TALKS TO: every other module - this is where they are wired together

text.font-family: Virgil, Segoe UI Emoji, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: STEP BY STEP (numbers match the badges)
1. You run a command; click calls the matching function.
2. attach / detach capture nothing themselves: they store the request (a
container name or a label) in SQLite.
3. A running `watch` daemon reads those requests on its next pass (within 5s) -
that's how one terminal steers a daemon running in another.
4. watch builds a CaptureManager (owns the tcpdumps) and a Selector (decides what
to capture), and first kills any tcpdump a crashed earlier run left behind.
5. It then runs 4 things side by side: the controller loop, the enrich loop that
turns pcaps into rows, a port sampler for host-network containers, and a
6. sidecar runs inside the target's network namespace. It checks eth0 exists and
refuses to start if the namespace is really the host's (a --network host
7. Its own 1-second loop keeps the capture healthy, and exits with code 3 when
the target stops, so the problem shows up in `docker ps`.
8. sidecars starts a Supervisor that manages sidecar containers through the
9. Read commands open the database, run a query from analyze.py / report.py,

• Starting the background threads and shutting them down: SIGTERM/SIGINT set a
stop flag; `finally` clears live_sessions and stops every tcpdump.
• Every background thread opens its OWN SQLite connection - a shared connection
once made the enrich thread die silently (see TODO.md).
• Each loop iteration is wrapped in try/except so a bug is logged and retried,

text.tspan: wakes a polling loop the moment Docker starts or stops a container

text.font-family: Virgil, Segoe UI Emoji, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: A small helper that makes the system react quickly. The controller and the supervisor normally check Docker every 5 seconds. This module opens
Docker's live event stream on a background thread and, whenever a container starts, dies or is removed, pokes the loop so it runs right away. It
decides nothing and passes no data along - it only says 'something changed, look now'. If the stream breaks it reconnects after 5s, and in the
meantime the normal 5-second polling keeps working, so nothing is missed.
OUT: a threading.Event that gets set
USED BY: watch (controller.run) and sidecars (the supervisor loop)

text.font-family: Virgil, Segoe UI Emoji, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: STEP BY STEP (numbers match the badges)
1. Docker publishes an event for every container change.
2. A background thread listens only for container start / die / destroy.
3. On each event it sets a shared flag (a threading.Event).
4. The loop waiting on that flag wakes early and reconciles now instead of
5. If the stream dies (Docker restarted, socket gone) it waits 5s and reconnects;

text.font-family: Virgil, Segoe UI Emoji, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: • Polling stays the source of truth. Events only cut the delay: a new container
is captured in about a second instead of up to 5s.
• A missed or dropped event costs at most one poll interval, so errors are only

text.tspan: reconciliation loop: makes running captures match the desired state (watch mode)

text.font-family: Virgil, Segoe UI Emoji, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: The brain of `watch` mode. It uses the 'reconcile' pattern (the same idea Kubernetes uses): keep a picture of what SHOULD be captured (desired state),
look at what IS being captured (actual state), and fix the difference. Desired state = containers matching the --label given at start-up, plus labels
and names added later with `nettap attach`. Each pass also restarts any tcpdump that crashed and applies the pcap disk limits. A pass runs every 5
seconds, or at once when events.py reports a container change. A failing pass is logged and the next one tries again, so a hiccup in the Docker API
IN: Docker's container list, the desired_refs / desired_labels tables
OUT: tcpdumps started / stopped (through capture.py), rows in containers and live_sessions
CALLED BY: `nettap watch` (cli.py), on the main thread

text.font-family: Virgil, Segoe UI Emoji, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: STEP BY STEP (numbers match the badges)
1. Wait for the next tick (5s) or an early wake-up from events.py.
2. Refresh the heartbeat in live_sessions so `nettap status` knows the daemon is
3. Ask the CaptureManager to restart any tcpdump that exited on its own.
4. Work out which containers should be captured: label match (CLI + database) or
5. Compare that with the containers being captured right now.
6. Missing one? Inspect it (discovery.py), save its details, start its tcpdump
7. Captured but not wanted any more (stopped, detached)? Stop its tcpdump and
8. Delete old pcaps if age / size limits are set, then go back to waiting.

text.font-family: Virgil, Segoe UI Emoji, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: • `nettap attach web` from another terminal only writes a DB row; the daemon
picks it up next cycle with no extra plumbing.
• A missed 'die' event can't leave a zombie capture running forever.
• Heartbeat runs before the main try: a failing Docker API doesn't mean captures
• Any exception in a pass is logged and the loop continues.

text.tspan: answers: which interface carries this container's traffic, and how do I reach it?

text.font-family: Virgil, Segoe UI Emoji, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: Before tcpdump can record a container, nettap must know WHERE that container's packets flow. Every container has its own network namespace (a private
network stack) connected to the host by a virtual cable called a veth pair: one end is eth0 inside the container, the other is an interface on the
host such as veth3a1f9c2. Capturing on that host end sees everything the container sends and receives - to the host, to other containers and to the
internet. This module reads the container from the Docker API, enters its namespace with nsenter to ask the kernel what kind of interface eth0 is, and
picks the best place to capture: the host-side veth (normal case), the container's own eth0 from inside (macvlan / ipvlan), every interface from
inside (several networks or a Swarm overlay), or the host's main interface filtered by port (--network host). The answer comes back as a
IN: a container ID, the Docker API, /var/run/docker/netns, /sys/class/net
OUT: ContainerNetInfo: where to capture, plus the container's IPs, ports, labels, start time
USED BY: controller.py (watch), and sidecar --docker-api to learn other containers' names

text.font-family: Virgil, Segoe UI Emoji, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: STEP BY STEP (numbers match the badges)
1. Read the container from the Docker API: name, IPs, ports, labels, and the
SandboxKey (the path to its network-namespace file).
2. Does it use --network host? Then it has no namespace of its own.
3. Yes: capture on the host's main interface, and later keep only its ports
4. No: enter its namespace and run `ip -j -d link` to learn eth0's type and the
index of the other end of its cable.
5. Decide by the type of link.
6. Several data interfaces (more than one network, Swarm overlay): capture all of
them but lo, inside the namespace.
7. macvlan / ipvlan have no veth: capture eth0 from inside the namespace.
8. veth: find the host interface with that index, check it points back at eth0,
9. Pack the answer and all metadata into a ContainerNetInfo.

text.font-family: Virgil, Segoe UI Emoji, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: • The host-side veth is the only door in or out of a container, so tcpdump on it
sees host, container-to-container and internet traffic.
• Nothing is installed in the target image: nettap enters its netns with the
• Not /sys/class/net/eth0/iflink: under nsenter --net sysfs still shows the
• sidecar calls this with resolve=False - it already sits in the target's netns.
split_by_netns() finds its target and peers by IP.

text.tspan: CaptureManager: owns one tcpdump per container (+ one for DNS) and its pcap files

text.font-family: Virgil, Segoe UI Emoji, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: Runs and looks after the tcpdump processes. For each container it starts one tcpdump on the interface discovery.py chose, writing raw packets to
data/pcap/<name>_<timestamp>.pcap and starting a new file every 60 seconds. It also starts a second, small tcpdump on the container's loopback (lo)
that records only lookups to Docker's built-in DNS server 127.0.0.11, because those never cross eth0. tcpdump flushes each packet straight to disk, so
the files can be read while they are still being written. The CaptureManager keeps a table of these processes so it can restart ones that crash, stop
them on detach, delete old files, and kill leftovers from an earlier crash.
OUT: tcpdump processes; .pcap and .dns.pcap files in data/pcap/ (open them in Wireshark)
CALLED BY: controller.py (watch) and the sidecar loop in cli.py

text.font-family: Virgil, Segoe UI Emoji, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: STEP BY STEP (numbers match the badges)
1. The controller or sidecar asks to capture a container.
2. Give up, with a log line, if there is no interface, or it's a host-network
container whose ports can't be attributed to it.
3. If the capture must run inside the container's namespace (watch mode), put
nsenter in front of the command.
4. Build the tcpdump command: interface, file-name pattern, new file every 60s
5. Start it. The kernel kills it if nettap dies (PDEATHSIG), and its error output
6. Start the second tcpdump on lo for DNS lookups to 127.0.0.11.
7. Both write rotating pcap files - the raw evidence everything else is built
8. Every pass: restart any tcpdump that exited.
9. Delete the oldest pcaps beyond the age / size limits.
10. At start-up: kill tcpdumps left running by a crashed earlier run (pids from
11. Stopping: SIGTERM, wait up to 5s, then SIGKILL.

text.font-family: Virgil, Segoe UI Emoji, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: • Called by controller / sidecar loop each pass. A tcpdump that dies quietly
would otherwise mean 'the report stopped updating' with no error.
WHY A SECOND CAPTURE ON LO
• Containers on user-defined networks ask 127.0.0.11 for DNS over lo, never eth0.
Filtered by host, not port: Docker NATs port 53 to a random port.
• Each packet is flushed to disk, so ingest.py can read a file while tcpdump is

text.tspan: feeds new packets to tshark every 5s, without waiting for a pcap to rotate

text.font-family: Virgil, Segoe UI Emoji, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: Turns growing pcap files into database rows within seconds. Waiting for a 60-second file to finish would make reports lag, so every 5 seconds this
module reads only the NEW part of each file. A pcap file is a 24-byte header followed by packets, each with its own 16-byte header that gives its
length. ingest walks those headers from where it stopped last time, stops before any packet tcpdump is still writing, copies the new packets (plus the
file header) into a small temporary pcap, and has enrich.py / tshark parse it. The rows and the new 'read up to here' position are saved in one
database transaction, so a crash, or two processes reading the same file, can never count a packet twice.
IN: pcap files, the pcap_progress table
OUT: rows in flows, updated offsets in pcap_progress
CALLED BY: the enrich loop in cli.py (every 5s) and the one-off `nettap enrich`

text.font-family: Virgil, Segoe UI Emoji, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: STEP BY STEP (numbers match the badges)
1. Every 5s, list every pcap file of every running capture.
2. Look up how far this file has been read (a byte offset) and whether it's
3. Walk the packet headers from that offset; stop at a half-written packet or one
4. Copy the file header + the new packets into a temporary pcap tshark can read.
6. Host-network container? Drop the packets that weren't on its ports
7. Save the rows and the new offset together; if another process already saved

text.font-family: Virgil, Segoe UI Emoji, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: • Rows and the new offset are saved in one transaction, so a packet is never
counted twice - after a restart, or when `nettap enrich` and the daemon look at
• final=True once a file has rotated: take every complete record and mark it
• The 2s hold-back gives the port sampler time to record a packet's port.
• A TLS ClientHello split across two chunks can lose its SNI.

text.tspan: thin tshark wrapper: one pcap in, one flow-row dict per packet out

text.font-family: Virgil, Segoe UI Emoji, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: The translator from raw packets to readable facts. It runs tshark (Wireshark's command-line tool) over a pcap and asks for 17 fields per packet: time,
source and destination IP (v4 or v6), ports, protocol name, size, the DNS question and answers, the TLS server name (SNI - the website name in an
HTTPS connection) and the HTTP Host header. It cleans each line into a Python dict - one row per packet - ready to insert into the flows table. It is
deliberately thin, so it could later be swapped for a richer tool such as Zeek.
IN: a pcap path, plus the container ID and name to tag rows with
OUT: a list of flow-row dicts

text.font-family: Virgil, Segoe UI Emoji, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: STEP BY STEP (numbers match the badges)
1. Receive a pcap (usually ingest's temporary chunk).
2. Run tshark with the field list; the output is CSV, with repeated values joined
3. Keep the first value of each field - an ICMP error packet carries a copy of
another packet's header that must be ignored.
4. Merge the IPv4/IPv6 and TCP/UDP columns into single src / dst / port fields,
5. Collect every DNS answer address into a JSON list (used later to put names on

text.font-family: Virgil, Segoe UI Emoji, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: • Its dissectors already get DNS, TLS SNI and HTTP Host right. Swapping to
Zeek/Suricata would only touch this file and FIELDS.
• tshark timeout (120s) or non-zero exit → logged, returns no rows.

text.tspan: port attribution for --network host targets, which have no netns of their own

text.font-family: Virgil, Segoe UI Emoji, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: Handles a special case. A container started with --network host shares the host's network, so a capture there sees traffic from the whole machine. To
keep only that container's traffic, nettap checks which TCP/UDP ports the container's processes hold, 4 times a second, and stores time ranges such as
'port 8080 belonged to web from 10:01 to 10:05'. When packets are ingested, keep_owned() keeps only those whose host-side port belonged to the
container at that moment. Sidecar mode finds the sockets through /proc for the target's processes; watch mode asks the kernel with `ss --cgroup` which
OUT: owned_ports rows; flow rows filtered down to the container's own
USED BY: the port-sampler threads in cli.py, and ingest.py

text.font-family: Virgil, Segoe UI Emoji, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: STEP BY STEP (numbers match the badges)
1. A sidecar started with --attribute-by-port, sharing the target's process
2. Read the socket list of every target process to see which ports it holds.
3. watch mode, for every host-network container it captures.
4. Run ss --cgroup and match each socket to a container by its cgroup path.
5. Every 0.25s, record the ports into owned_ports as time intervals.
6. During ingest, keep a packet only if its host-side port was owned at that
7. Everything else (other containers, the host itself) is dropped.

text.font-family: Virgil, Segoe UI Emoji, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: • A host-network capture sees the whole Docker host. Without filtering, every
container's traffic would be labelled as the target.
• A connection opened and closed between two samples is missed; listening ports
are reliable, short outgoing requests may not be.
• ICMP and ARP are dropped (no port). ss needs nettap in the host's cgroup

text.tspan: SQLite: the flow store, plus the tables separate nettap processes coordinate through

text.font-family: Virgil, Segoe UI Emoji, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: All persistent state lives in one SQLite file (data/nettap.db). Besides storing packet rows, the database is how separate nettap processes talk to
each other: `nettap attach` writes a request into desired_*, and the watch daemon reads it; the daemon writes what it's capturing into live_sessions,
and `nettap status` reads it. This module creates the tables (and adds new columns to older databases), and offers a small function for each read and
write so other modules don't write raw SQL for these tables. The diagram shows each table with who writes it (left) and who reads it (right).
USED BY: almost every module - each thread opens its own connection

text.font-family: Virgil, Segoe UI Emoji, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: STEP BY STEP (numbers match the badges)
1. Requests from attach / detach: container names / IDs and labels to capture.
2. What a daemon is capturing now: tcpdump pids, file patterns and a heartbeat
time (a stale row means the daemon died).
3. Facts about each container: name, IP per network, published ports, start time
- used to put names on IPs.
4. The main data: one row per packet with IPs, ports, protocol, size, DNS, SNI,
5. How far each pcap has been parsed, so parsing resumes without duplicates.
6. When each port belonged to a host-network container.

text.font-family: Virgil, Segoe UI Emoji, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: • SQLite is also the message bus: `nettap attach` in one terminal steers a
`nettap watch` daemon in another just by writing rows.
• connect() creates missing tables and adds columns added after a table's first
• store_pcap_chunk() is the only atomic multi-step write (rows + offset).
• insert_flows / query boundary kept narrow so swapping to Postgres/ClickHouse

text.tspan: nettap sidecars: keeps exactly one sidecar container per labelled target

text.font-family: Virgil, Segoe UI Emoji, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: Powers `nettap sidecars`, which automates sidecar mode. A sidecar must share its target's network namespace, and Docker ties that to one particular
container instance: if the target stops, the sidecar dies; if the target is recreated, the old sidecar points at nothing. The supervisor checks Docker
every 5s (and on events) and keeps exactly one healthy sidecar per labelled container: it creates missing ones, starts or restarts ones that fell out
of step, replaces ones whose target was recreated, and removes ones whose target is gone. A sidecar that crashed for another reason is left alone, so
it isn't restarted in a loop.
IN: the Docker API: all containers with their labels and state
OUT: sidecar containers created / started / restarted / removed

text.font-family: Virgil, Segoe UI Emoji, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: STEP BY STEP (numbers match the badges)
1. Run a pass on every tick or Docker event.
2. List the containers and split them into targets (label match) and our sidecars
3. Compare each target with its sidecar.
4. No sidecar yet: create nettap-sidecar-<name> sharing the target's network.
5. The sidecar was made for an older container with that name: replace it.
6. The target restarted after its sidecar started: restart the sidecar so it
7. The sidecar exited because its target stopped (code 3): start it again.
8. The sidecar crashed for another reason: warn once and leave it alone.
9. Finally, remove sidecars whose target no longer exists or no longer matches.

text.font-family: Virgil, Segoe UI Emoji, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: • A sidecar joins its target's netns once. When the target stops, Docker removes
the shared eth0 and the sidecar exits (code 3); Docker restart policies give up
• Sidecars carry labels nettap.sidecar.target / target-id / selector, so two
supervisors with different selectors leave each other alone.
• A crashing sidecar isn't restarted in a loop. On shutdown, sidecars are stopped
(pcaps flushed) and removed in parallel, unless --keep-sidecars.

text.tspan: read-side SQL over flows + containers; output is JSON or a table

text.font-family: Virgil, Segoe UI Emoji, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: Answers questions about the captured traffic with SQL over the flows and containers tables. Who talked the most? Which containers talk to each other?
Which internet addresses and hostnames were contacted? What DNS lookups happened? Which protocols were used? Helper functions do the tricky parts:
deciding which container owned an IP when a packet was sent (IPs get reused when containers are recreated), whether an IP is on the internet or local,
and the best name for an IP (from TLS SNI, HTTP Host or DNS answers). Results are lists of dicts, printed as JSON or a table, and report.py reuses
IN: the flows and containers tables
OUT: lists of dicts (JSON, or a table with --format table)

text.font-family: Virgil, Segoe UI Emoji, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: STEP BY STEP (numbers match the badges)
1. Start from the stored flow rows and container facts.
2. Map an IP to the container that held it when the packet was sent.
3. Classify an IP as internet or local, with hints such as 'Docker Desktop DNS'.
4. Find a hostname for each IP from SNI, HTTP Host or DNS answers.
5. Biggest source → destination pairs by bytes.
6. Container-to-container traffic, direct or through a published port.
7. Traffic leaving Docker: destinations that belong to no container, with names.
8. The DNS names that were looked up.
10. Print as JSON (for scripts) or an aligned table (for people).

text.font-family: Virgil, Segoe UI Emoji, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: • Each flow belongs to the capture it came from (container_name). The peer is
found by matching dst_ip to a container's address at the packet's time - IPs
get reused when containers are recreated.
• Traffic to the host on a port another container publishes counts as container-
• `nettap analyze ...` directly, and report.py for the plain-language summary.
top_talkers, dns_queries and protocol_breakdown read flows directly.

text.tspan: turns analyze output into a summary a non-technical reader can follow

text.font-family: Virgil, Segoe UI Emoji, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: Writes a summary for someone who doesn't know networking: how much the container sent and received, which other containers and internet sites it
talked to (with names), what it looked up in DNS, and which protocols it used. It gathers the numbers with analyze.py into one dict, separates
internet destinations from local ones, and renders either plain text for the terminal or one self-contained HTML file you can double-click (no server
IN: a container name, the SQLite database
OUT: text on the terminal, or an .html file in the data directory

text.font-family: Virgil, Segoe UI Emoji, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: STEP BY STEP (numbers match the badges)
1. Pick a container, and text or HTML.
2. Count total packets and bytes, find its own IPs, split bytes into sent and
3. Get peers, external destinations, DNS lookups and the protocol mix from
4. Split destinations into internet and local network.
5. Render readable sentences for the terminal.
6. Render one HTML file with inline styles and bar charts.

• Port-scoped captures get a note saying traffic was picked out by port.
